title: Hierarchy of Road Users & Vulnerable Users
whatItIs: The hierarchy puts those most at risk at the top. Those who can cause the greatest harm carry the greatest responsibility.
keyFacts: Most at risk: pedestrians, cyclists, horse riders, motorcyclists; children, older and disabled people more so.
H1: those driving vehicles that can cause the greatest harm bear the greatest responsibility.
H2: at a junction, give way to pedestrians crossing or waiting to cross.

keyFacts.text: You MUST give way to pedestrians on a zebra, and to pedestrians and cyclists on a parallel crossing.

keyFacts: H3: don't cut across cyclists or horse riders going ahead when you turn or change lane.

keyFacts.text: You MUST stop when a school crossing patrol shows a 'Stop for children' sign.

points: Don't wave, flash or hoot to invite them

onTheTest.question: Your pupil is turning left. A cyclist goes straight ahead in a cycle lane alongside. What should they do?
options: Wait for the cyclist to pass
onTheTest.why: Rule H3: don't cut across cyclists going ahead when turning, whether in a cycle lane, a cycle track or on the road. Don't turn if they'd have to stop or swerve.

onTheTest.question: A pedestrian has a white cane with a red band. What does it tell you?
onTheTest.why: Rule 207: deafblind people may carry a white cane with a red band or use a dog with a red and white harness. They may not see or hear signals.

traps: The hierarchy doesn't remove anyone's duty to behave responsibly.
Cyclists may ride in the centre of the lane on narrow roads: allow it.
Turning right across a queue? Look for riders on the inside.
Pedestrians who've started to cross at a junction have priority: wait.
